items.title: How RNA molecules influence the development of aggressive leukemia
items.text: Researchers at the University of Veterinary Medicine Vienna, in collaboration with the CeMM Research Center for Molecular Medicine and St. Anna Children's Cancer Research, have developed a new analytical method that reveals which RNA molecules are involved in cancer-promoting cellular structures. Using this method, the Vienna-based research team identified the RNA molecule Gas5 as an important regulator of NUP98::KDM5A oncogenic condensates, which control gene activity in aggressive forms of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This new insight may provide important starting points for cancer research and improved patient treatment. The study was published in the journal The EMBO Journal.

items.title: Simple, noninvasive technique can assess collagen in the skin of scleroderma patients
items.text: Scleroderma (systemic sclerosis) is a rare, chronic autoimmune disease that causes the body to produce too much collagen, leading to the hardening and thickening of the skin and internal organs. For more than 50 years, physicians have relied on manually pinching the skin to assess its thickness, a subjective approach that remains central to the diagnosis of systemic sclerosis, assessment of disease extent and progression and monitoring of response to treatment.

items.title: Medical device adverse event reports are often incomplete, inaccurate and delayed
items.text: Permitting medical device manufacturers to submit bulk summary reports of adverse events to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), rather than reporting individual cases, often fails to promptly detect potential safety signals, finds a study published by The BMJ. This is a public health concern, argue the researchers, and they call for immediate improvements to better protect patient safety and meet FDA standards.
